extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, dramatists, and writers studying story craft (especially for film)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing scenes and overall story shape for film: use of suspense/mystery/irony, surprise, coincidence, comedy design, point of view, and adaptation of other media to screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: In Suspense the audience and characters know the same information. Suspense combines both Curiosity and Concern. In Suspense curiosity is not about fact but outcome; the outcome may end 'up' or 'down' or in irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters and audience move shoulder to shoulder through the telling, sharing the same knowledge. As characters discover expositional fact, the audience discovers it. What no one knows is 'How will this turn out?' This relationship creates empathy and identification with the protagonist (unlike Mystery, which elicits only sympathy). Example: many films, comedy and drama, compel interest primarily in this mode (about 90% of films).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery (Closed Mystery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery begins as a 'Who done it?' where the audience lacks certain facts; curiosity is about fact rather than outcome. The outcome of a Murder Mystery is always certain (e.g., the detective will catch the killer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mysteries restrict audience knowledge of facts to pique intellectual curiosity. Master detectives are charming but rarely in real jeopardy, so the audience tends toward sympathy rather than identification. Treat Murder Mysteries like puzzles/board games—cool entertainments for the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic Irony
rubrics_metrics.description: In Dramatic Irony the audience knows more than the characters. It creates interest primarily through concern and dread, often eliminating curiosity about facts and outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic Irony frequently opens with the ending (giving away outcome), switching audience emotion from anxiety to dread and compassion for characters heading toward disaster. It encourages asking 'How and why did these characters do what I already know they did?' and directs attention to motivations, inner life, unconscious energies, and social forces. Examples: SUNSET BOULEVARD, BETRAYAL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing Mystery, Suspense, and Dramatic Irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Most genres do not lend themselves to pure Mystery or pure Dramatic Irony; writers often mix the three within an overall Suspense design to enrich the telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within one story, some sequences can employ Mystery to increase curiosity about certain facts, and other sequences can switch to Dramatic Irony to heighten compassion and dread. Example: CASABLANCA uses Dramatic Irony (flashback to the affair) and later switches to Mystery (Rick's Crisis decision is kept from audience) to jolt the viewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of strategy at Climax (three tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: At a Story Climax you can employ Mystery (hide a fact from the audience), Suspense (audience and characters share the same information), or Dramatic Irony (audience knows a fact hidden from the protagonist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (corridor/axe murderer scene): Mystery: close doors and hide the killer's location to make audience search. Suspense: let audience and protagonist both see the danger (shadow behind a door) and retain uncertainty about outcome. Dramatic Irony: show the killer behind a closed door unknown to the protagonist, switching audience emotion to dread. Be careful: false outcomes like an anticlimax ('it was just wood-chopping husband') are Cheap Surprise/False Mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid False Mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: False Mystery is a counterfeit curiosity caused by artificial concealment of fact that should have been given to the audience, withheld in hope of holding interest over long, undramatized passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not withhold exposition that could and should be given; example anti-pattern: long prelude flashback meant only to delay the promised action (pilot crash flashback). The audience will tune out in frustration if you abuse concealment. Reward the filmgoer with honest, insightful answers to their questions—no dirty tricks, no cheap surprise, no False Mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Surprise vs Cheap Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of surprise: True surprise springs from the sudden revelation of the Gap between expectation and result and is followed by insight. Cheap Surprise is a jolt or shock that breaks narrative flow without delivering meaningful tragedy or insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True surprise reveals a deeper truth of the fictional world. Cheap surprise can momentarily shock but lacks tragic or insightful consequence and is generally a shoddy device outside certain genre conventions. In Horror, Fantasy, Thriller cheap surprise can be a convention and part of the fun; elsewhere avoid it. Aristotle's complaint: to threaten action and then not act is merely shocking, not tragic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidence is not inherently forbidden; it is part of life but is by definition random and meaningless unless dramatized to gain meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First, bring coincidence in early so you have time to build meaning from it (e.g., JAWS inciting incident: random shark attack becomes meaningful as the menace stays). Second, do not use coincidence to turn an ending—this is deus ex machina and insults the audience. Use coincidence to seed later causal meaning or to dramatize the absurd when coincidence rules story (Antistructure films). Example contrast: a one-off helpful real-estate agent is pointless coincidence; an agent leading to spotting a red Maserati that becomes recurring antagonism can build meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never use deus ex machina to resolve story
rubrics_metrics.description: Deus ex machina (an act of god or sudden external contrivance that resolves story problems) erases meaning and emotion and is an insult to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: ancient playwrights used gods to resolve climaxes; contemporary writers use 'acts of god' (hurricane, stampede, sudden accident, or last-minute creature). Such resolutions remove character responsibility and choice; avoid them except when deliberately creating Antistructure meaning (life-as-absurd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy principles: what makes a Comedy succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is pure: If the audience laughs, it works; if it doesn’t, it doesn’t. Comedy attacks institutions or social hypocrisy, and its comic sensibility arises from frustrated idealism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often focuses on social institutions (ruling class, military, courtship, etc.). Comic Design allows halting Narrative Drive to interpolate scenes with no story purpose purely for laughs (LITTLE SHOP OF HORRORS, Marx Brothers). Comedy tolerates more coincidence and may accept deus ex machina endings provided two things: (1) the protagonist has suffered enormously, and (2) he never despairs, keeping hope. For writing gags start from Turning Points: ask 'What’s the opposite of that?' then 'What’s off-the-wall?' to create comic gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic structure vs dramatic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an elaborate rolling joke; wit alone doesn't make a Comedy. True comedy makes people laugh from the pitch of the story itself (pitch the series of events and hear laughter repeatedly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can tell the story events aloud (without quoting dialogue) and it consistently elicits laughter at each turn, you've written a Comedy. Otherwise the work may be a hybrid (dramedy, crimedy). Focus comedic surprises on turning points and escalate the gaps between expectation and result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of View within a scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of View (POV) is the physical angle from which a scene is imagined; choices within a scene strongly influence audience empathy and reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four distinctive choices: (1) follow one character exclusively (center imagination on Jack), (2) follow the other character exclusively (center on Tony), (3) alternate between their POVs, (4) take a neutral/distant POV (in profile). Each choice changes what audience empathizes with: first encourages empathy for Jack, second for Tony, third for both, fourth encourages detachment or laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of View for the whole story (protagonist's POV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Styling the whole story from the protagonist's Point of View—disciplining the tale to the protagonist's experience—generally enhances audience empathy and yields a tight, memorable narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the more difficult approach (limits hopscotching through time/space) but is a creative discipline that rewards with a deeper relationship between audience and character. More time with a character offers more opportunity to witness choices, increasing empathy and emotional involvement. The easy way (jumping around) risks sprawl and loss of tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium strengths: novel, theatre, cinema (adaptation principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each medium tells complex stories by conflicts on inner, personal, and extra-personal levels, but each medium has a distinctive strength: novel = inner conflict; theatre = personal conflict; cinema = extra-personal conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these strengths, 'purer' works (novels concentrated on inner life, plays concentrated on personal, theatrical language) are the hardest to adapt to film. Film excels at huge vivid images and extra-personal conflict (e.g., chase sequences), while theatre can use poetic dialogue and soliloquy more freely, and novels can slip inside thought with density and imagery. Respect the medium when adapting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation first principle: purer the source, the worse for film
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to adapt 'pure' literature or theatre often fail because image/cinema lacks equivalents for densely inner or poetically theatrical material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'pure' novel (inner conflict dominant) or 'pure' play (personal conflict in poetic language) resists cinematic conversion; adapting such works often requires reinvention and risking deviation from the original in order to make an excellent film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation process and reinvention (practical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To adapt: (1) read the work repeatedly to absorb its spirit; (2) reduce each event to a one- or two-sentence statement of what happens (no psychology/sociology); (3) read events and ask 'Is this story well told?'; (4) be willing to reinvent—reorder events chronologically, create a step-outline, cut or invent scenes, and turn mental material into physical action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rush into making choices; first feel the society and characters. Most adaptations demand reinvention: test whether the original writer's storytelling works in filmic rhythms, and be prepared to deviate. If you reinvent radically and produce an excellent film, critics will accept it; if you butcher the original, you'll be criticized. Study master adapters (e.g., Ruth Prawer Jhabvala) to see how to restrict source material to camera-attractive conflicts and express inner life visually rather than through explanatory dialogue.
